# Writing the manuscript



By now we have judged whether a question is viable, registered it, and fitted
a curve. What remains is the part reviewers actually read. In this chapter we
walk through the main parts of the manuscript and of the supplementary
material, in the order they appear on the page, and we say what belongs in
each one.

Much of the content has already been built in the earlier chapters. Where that
is so, we point back rather than repeat ourselves, and we spend the space here
on the one thing no earlier chapter covers: how to put the work on the page so
that a reader can check it.

## The checklist

A dose-response review is reported under **PRISMA** like any other systematic
review [@page2021]. Yet PRISMA knows nothing about dose levels, reference
categories or spline knots. The table below is therefore the short supplement
to it: what a dose-response manuscript carries that a conventional one does
not.


::: {#tbl-checklist .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='What belongs in each part of a dose-response manuscript. This supplements the PRISMA checklist rather than replacing it.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Section                |What belongs there                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|:----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|Introduction           |Why the shape matters, and not only whether the exposure matters. The decision a curve would inform. The registration number.                                                                                                                                                           |
|Methods                |Eligibility, including the three-level rule. Search and dates. What was extracted per dose level. How doses were assigned and harmonised. The reference category rule. Model, shape, knots. Heterogeneity, bias, subgroups and sensitivity. Software with versions, and the repository. |
|Results                |Study and participant counts. The dose range covered. Table 1 and Table 2. The pooled trend, the test for departure from linearity, heterogeneity, and the curve. Subgroups and sensitivity as pre-specified.                                                                           |
|Discussion             |What the shape means on the dose scale. Comparison with published curves. Where the evidence thins out. Limitations specific to dose-response, including the unit of analysis and dose harmonisation.                                                                                   |
|Conclusion             |One or two sentences answering the question that was asked, at a named dose, without leaving the observed range.                                                                                                                                                                        |
|Supplementary material |Full search strings. Outcome definitions per study. The dose conversion table. Risk of bias per domain. Leave-one-out and the shapes not chosen. The analysis code.                                                                                                                     |
|Proposed figures       |PRISMA flow, forest of study trends, the dose-response curve, subgroup curves.                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|Proposed tables        |Table 1 with study and participant characteristics, Table 2 with the effect at the doses of interest.                                                                                                                                                                                   |


:::
:::


Let us take the rows in order.

## Introduction

Two sentences carry a dose-response introduction that a conventional one does
not. The first says why the shape matters. The second says what decision would
change if the shape were known.

We made that argument in full in Chapter 1: a single pooled estimate answers
"does it matter" and cannot answer "how much". The introduction is where the
argument is made for one specific exposure, briefly, and then dropped.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Example**

> _Meta-analyses of alcohol and cardiovascular disease have pooled the highest
> reported intake against the lowest. That contrast answers whether drinkers
> differ from non-drinkers, and it cannot say how risk changes across the
> range of intake. Public health guidance is written in grams per day, so the
> quantity that matters for guidance is the shape of the relationship rather
> than a single contrast. We therefore estimated the dose-response
> relationship between alcohol intake and cardiovascular disease (PROSPERO
> CRD420XXXXXXXX)._

Three sentences, three jobs: the gap, why the shape is the decision-relevant
quantity, and the registration number from Chapter 3.
:::

@bryazka2022 is worth reading as a model. Its introduction does not argue that
alcohol matters. It argues that the dose question is open, which is what earns
the paper its method.

## Methods

The longest section, and almost all of it has been built already. Chapter 2
covered extraction and the reference category, Chapter 3 the protocol and the
risk of bias, Chapter 4 the model itself.

What we add here is the reminder that each of those decisions has to appear in
the manuscript, and not only in the protocol. A reader cannot check the
registration against the paper if the paper leaves out the thing that was
registered.

The order that reads well:

1. Protocol and registration
2. Eligibility, including the three-level rule and what happened to the
   studies that fell below it
3. Search, databases and dates, with the full strings in the supplement
4. Extraction, one row per dose level per study, and what was taken per level
5. Dose assignment and harmonisation, including the open-ended top category
6. The reference category, and what was done when studies disagreed
7. The model: one-stage or two-stage, covariance method, shape, knots
8. Heterogeneity, publication bias, sensitivity and subgroups
9. Software, package versions, and where the code lives

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Example**

The statistical paragraph, written out in full in Chapter 4, reduces to this
shape:

> _We fitted a two-stage random-effects dose-response model. Within-study
> covariances between estimates sharing a reference category were
> reconstructed by the method of Greenland and Longnecker. The dose-response
> relationship was modelled with a restricted cubic spline with three knots
> placed at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of the observed intake
> distribution, specified in the protocol before any data were extracted.
> Departure from linearity was tested with a Wald test on the spline terms._

Every clause names a decision a reader is free to disagree with, which is the
point of writing it out.
:::

## Results

The results section has a fixed running order, and it is the order of the
figures. One paragraph of characteristics comes first: how many studies, how
many participants and cases, the dose range the pooled data covers, and which
designs are included.

Then the pooled result itself: the trend, the test for departure from
linearity, and the heterogeneity. Let us read those numbers off the fitted
model rather than retype them, because a number retyped by hand is a number
that can disagree with its own figure.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Example**

> _Six study contrasts contributed 25 intake categories covering 0 to 77.2
> grams per day. The restricted cubic spline showed a departure from
> linearity, with risk lowest at moderate intake and rising at higher intake.
> Estimates at 10, 25 and 50 grams per day are given in Table 2, and the
> fitted curve in Figure 3._

We see what the paragraph does not do. It does not interpret, it does not
recommend an intake, and it says nothing about what happens beyond 77.2 grams
per day.
:::

## Discussion

The discussion is where a dose-response paper most often goes wrong, because a
curve invites claims that a curve cannot support. Three things belong here and
nowhere else.

**What the shape means on the dose scale.** Not "alcohol was associated with
cardiovascular disease", which the curve did not test, but what happens
between two named intakes.

**Comparison with published curves.** Dose-response results are comparable to
each other in a way that pooled estimates are not, because both are functions
of the same quantity. Where another review fitted the same exposure, the two
curves can be laid side by side.

**Limitations specific to this design.** Three of them recur: the unit of
analysis issue from Chapter 1, dose harmonisation across studies that defined
their categories differently, and the width of the band where the data thin
out.

::: {.callout-important}
**The claim a curve does not support**

A curve is estimated over the range the studies reported, and its band widens
wherever they thin out. Reading a threshold off the point where the band
crosses the null is the commonest error in this literature, because that point
moves with the width of the band and not only with the size of the effect.

The Burden of Proof papers [@gbd2022tobacco; @gbd2022vegetables] and the
critique of them [@burdenofproofconcerns2023] are the best available case
study. We recommend reading that exchange before writing a discussion that
names an optimal dose.
:::

## Conclusion

One or two sentences. They answer the question the introduction asked, at a
named dose, inside the observed range.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Example**

> _Across the intake range these studies report, cardiovascular risk was
> lowest at moderate intake and did not fall further at higher intake. The
> data do not support a recommendation above the observed range._

The second sentence is the one co-authors tend to cut, and it is the one that
should stay.
:::

## The supplementary material

The supplement is where a dose-response review becomes checkable. Six things
belong in it.

1. **Full search strings**, verbatim, per database, with the dates they were run.
2. **Outcome definitions per study**, because studies that call an outcome by
   the same name often do not measure the same thing.
3. **The dose conversion table**, showing how each study turned its categories
   into numbers, including the rule used for the open-ended top category.
4. **Risk of bias per domain per study**, as described in Chapter 3.
5. **Sensitivity analyses**: leave-one-out, and the alternative shapes that
   were fitted but not chosen.
6. **The analysis code**, so that the curve can be re-run rather than re-read.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Supplementary figure: leave-one-out. Each row refits the model without one study, which shows whether the result rests on a single contributor.](05-checklist-writing_files/figure-html/fig-loo-1.png){#fig-loo fig-align='center' width=864}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Example: the outcome definition table**

A supplementary table whose only job is to let a reader see that the studies
are not quite measuring the same thing.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Study   |Outcome as defined in the paper                                |
|:-------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
|Study A |Non-fatal myocardial infarction, hospital discharge code       |
|Study B |Death from coronary heart disease, death certificate           |
|Study C |Incident coronary heart disease, self-report with record check |
|Study D |Incident coronary heart disease, adjudicated by committee      |


:::
:::


The wording here is illustrative. The column that matters is the second one,
and writing it out usually changes what goes into the limitations.
:::

## The figures

Let us look at the figures one by one. Four figures in the paper, in this order. The order is not decoration: the
numbering is the running order of the results, and reviewers expect it.

### Figure 1. The PRISMA flow

The standard flow diagram, with one difference that matters. The exclusion
reasons at the full-text stage should name the dose-response ones separately.
"Fewer than three dose levels" and "no counts per level" are the two a reviewer
looks for, because together they say whether the viability check of Chapter 2
was applied at all.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Figure 1: study flow, with exclusion reasons specific to a dose-response review. The counts are illustrative; the structure and the named reasons are the point.](05-checklist-writing_files/figure-html/fig-prisma-1.png){#fig-prisma fig-align='center' width=720}
:::
:::


### Figure 2. The forest of study trends

Not a forest of contrasts. One row per study, each row carrying that study's
trend together with its number of dose levels and the range it covers. A
reader sees at a glance which studies could carry a trend at all.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Figure 2: one dose-response trend per study, with the number of levels and the dose range each one covers.](05-checklist-writing_files/figure-html/fig-forest-1.png){#fig-forest fig-align='center' width=960}
:::
:::


### Figure 3. The dose-response curve

The figure the paper exists for. Its caption carries the reference dose, the
band, the shape with its knots, and the test for departure from linearity.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Figure 3: the fitted dose-response curve for the main outcome, with its 95% confidence band. Reference 0 g/day, restricted cubic spline, knots as printed in the subtitle.](05-checklist-writing_files/figure-html/fig-curve-1.png){#fig-curve fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


### Figure 4. Subgroup curves

Pre-specified subgroups, drawn on shared axes so that the strata can be
compared by eye. Here the natural subgroup is study design, since the table
mixes case-control data with cumulative incidence.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Figure 4: the curve by study design. Strata on common axes, so that the comparison is visual as well as numerical.](05-checklist-writing_files/figure-html/fig-subgroup-1.png){#fig-subgroup fig-align='center' width=720}
:::
:::


We see two strata that separate only at the higher intakes, and the table
under the plot gives the slope and the test for each one. A difference
between strata is tested, never read off two overlapping bands.

### Getting the figures out of R

Each of the four figures writes itself to a file when it is given one. The
format is `filetype`, which is `"png"` unless a journal asks for `"tiff"` or
`"pdf"`, the folder is `path`, and the name is `file.name`. The size is
measured from the figure, so a forest of twenty studies comes out taller than
one of six, and `width` and `height` are there for the journal that specifies
its own. The README and Chapter 4 show the calls.

## The tables

Two tables belong in the paper. More than two usually means something belongs
in the supplement instead.

### Table 1. Studies and participants

One row per study: the design, how many intake categories it reported, the
range those categories cover, and the people behind them. This is the table
that lets a reader judge the evidence before seeing any estimate.


::: {#tbl-baseline .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Table 1: characteristics of the included studies and participants.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|Study             |Design               | Levels|Dose range | Cases|    N|
|:-----------------|:--------------------|------:|:----------|-----:|----:|
|Bianchi           |case-control         |      5|0 to 64.8  |   297|  981|
|Bobak             |case-control         |      4|0 to 77.2  |   202|  937|
|Malarcher-beer    |case-control         |      4|0 to 15.6  |   162|  445|
|Malarcher-wine    |case-control         |      4|0 to 18.7  |   150|  452|
|Vliegenthart-beer |cumulative incidence |      4|0 to 30    |   465| 1795|
|Vliegenthart-wine |cumulative incidence |      4|0 to 28.8  |   465| 1795|


:::
:::


### Table 2. The effect at the doses of interest

The doses are chosen in the protocol, not after seeing the curve. They are
usually the intakes that existing guidance already speaks about.


::: {#tbl-doses .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Table 2: the fitted effect at the pre-specified intakes, with confidence and prediction intervals.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


| Dose (g/day)|   OR| 95% CI low| 95% CI high| 95% PI low| 95% PI high|
|------------:|----:|----------:|-----------:|----------:|-----------:|
|            0| 1.00|       1.00|        1.00|       1.00|        1.00|
|           10| 0.81|       0.69|        0.94|       0.57|        1.14|
|           25| 0.74|       0.56|        0.98|       0.40|        1.38|
|           50| 1.50|       0.39|        5.74|       0.04|       58.59|


:::
:::


`easydr_table()` is the function that builds it. It takes the fit and the
doses, adds the reference dose because every other row is measured against it,
and marks any row that falls beyond the range the studies reported. Given a
`filetype` and a `file.name` it writes the same table to a spreadsheet or to a
PDF, which is the form a journal asks for. `main` is the title it carries.

The prediction interval is wider than the confidence interval on purpose. It
is the interval a new study would be expected to fall in, and it is the honest
number to quote when somebody asks what to expect next.

## Cite the tools, and the repository

::: {.callout-important}
**This part is not optional**

A dose-response curve is the product of several modelling decisions taken
inside software. A methods section that says "analyses were performed in R"
does not let anybody reproduce it, and a reader cannot tell which covariance
approximation, which shape, or which knot rule produced the figure.

Name all of it, with versions:

- **{easyDR}**, this package, together with the repository that holds both the
  package and this book: <https://github.com/vanioljantunes/easyDR>
- **{dosresmeta}** [@crippa2016], which does the estimation
- the method itself [@greenland1992]
- _R_, with its version number

The [Cite this material](cite.qmd) page carries the exact wording for the
first of these, generated from the installed version. Copy it rather than
retyping it, because the version number is the part that matters most and the
part most often got wrong.
:::

The package prints its own call back on request, which is the quickest way to
get every argument into the methods sentence without missing one.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Example**

> _Analyses were performed in R. Dose-response models were fitted with the
> easyDR package (version 0.0.0.9000;
> https://github.com/vanioljantunes/easyDR), which prepares the data and calls
> dosresmeta (Crippa and Orsini, 2016) for estimation using the method of
> Greenland and Longnecker (1992). The analysis code is available in the
> supplementary material._
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Test your knowledge!**

1. A co-author proposes reporting the intake at which the confidence band
   first crosses the null, and calling it a threshold. What is wrong with
   that, and what would you report instead?
2. Why does the forest plot of a dose-response paper carry one row per study
   rather than one row per intake category?
3. A reviewer asks why Table 2 reports a prediction interval as well as a
   confidence interval. What is the one-sentence answer?
4. Which three limitations are specific to a dose-response review and belong
   in every discussion?

Answers to these questions are listed in Appendix A.
:::

## Summary

- A dose-response review is reported under PRISMA, plus the items in
  @tbl-checklist that PRISMA does not cover: dose assignment, the reference
  category, the shape and its knots.
- The results section has a fixed running order, and the figure numbering is
  that order: flow, study trends, the curve, subgroups.
- Two tables belong in the paper. Table 1 describes the studies and the
  participants, and Table 2 reports the effect at intakes chosen in the
  protocol.
- The supplement carries what makes the review checkable: search strings,
  outcome definitions, the dose conversion table, risk of bias, leave-one-out,
  the shapes that were not chosen, and the code.
- The conclusion answers the question at a named dose, inside the observed
  range, and says so plainly when the data do not reach further.
- Software, package versions and the repository belong in the methods. A curve
  reported without them is a figure that nobody can reproduce.

::: {.cta}
**This chapter is the written half of a class.** The [Meta-Analysis
Academy](https://metahub.metaanalysisacademy.com) course walks through the same
material on video, with the worked example built live, the templates ready to
fill, and somewhere to ask when your data does not look like the example.

Found an error, or something explained badly? [Open an
issue](https://github.com/vanioljantunes/easyDR/issues) — corrections are
welcome and credited.
:::
